title: Divorce, Pledges, Wages, and What Is Left for the Poor
summary: Moses regulates divorce by forbidding a man to remarry a wife he divorced after she has married another. He exempts a newly married man from war for a year, forbids kidnapping, and gives a series of laws protecting the poor: no taking a millstone as a pledge, returning a poor man's cloak by sunset, paying a hired worker each day, justice for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and leaving the forgotten sheaf and the last olives and grapes for them.
story: The law code is nearing its end (it closes with chapter 26), and its concern for the vulnerable becomes sharper. Chapter 24 moves between marriage, debt, labor, and harvest, but the same people keep appearing: a divorced wife, a new bride, a poor borrower, a day laborer, and the trio of foreigner, fatherless, and widow. Twice the chapter tells Israel to remember that it was once enslaved in Egypt. The laws look back to the exodus and forward to life in the land, and they shape later stories directly. The book of Ruth is built on the gleaning law of verse 19, and Jesus' teaching on divorce begins from verse 1.
historical:
The divorce law of verses 1-4 does not institute divorce; it assumes the practice and regulates one case. Divorce by written document was known across the ancient Near East, and a certificate protected the woman by proving she was free to remarry. The key phrase, some indecency, became a famous point of dispute. By the first century, according to the Mishnah (Gittin 9:10), the school of Shammai held that it meant sexual unfaithfulness, while the school of Hillel allowed divorce for much lesser causes. That debate is the background to the Pharisees' question to Jesus in Matthew 19:3.

Verse 16, which forbids executing children for their fathers' crimes, is cited in the history of Judah. When King Amaziah executed the officials who had murdered his father, he spared their sons according to this law (2 Kings 14:5-6). The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel both developed the principle that each person dies for his own sin (Jeremiah 31:29-30; Ezekiel 18).
cultural:
Village life in Israel depended on a few essential goods. A hand mill made of two stones ground the grain for each day's bread, so taking the millstones as a pledge for a debt was, as verse 6 says, taking a person's livelihood. A poor man's cloak served as his blanket at night, so it had to be returned by sunset. A lender was not to enter the borrower's house to choose his pledge, protecting the borrower's dignity. Hired laborers lived day to day and needed their pay before evening to buy food.

The foreigner (a resident alien without family land), the fatherless, and the widow were the three groups most likely to fall through the gaps of a society built on family inheritance. Deuteronomy names them together again and again. Harvesting was done by hand, and the law told farmers not to go back for a forgotten sheaf or to beat the olive branches or strip the vines a second time. What was left belonged to the poor, who could glean it with their own labor rather than depend on handouts. The story of Ruth shows this law at work in Boaz's field.
literary: The chapter is a set of case laws and short commands, many of them paired with a motive clause that explains why. Some reasons point to God's blessing, some to the poor man's blessing, and the strongest point back to Egypt: Remember that you were slaves (verses 18 and 22). The two reminders frame the final section on justice and gleaning. Verses 10-13 and 14-15 both turn on sunset, when the cloak must be returned and the wage must be paid. Verse 9 briefly recalls Miriam, who was struck with a skin disease after speaking against Moses (Numbers 12), as a warning to take the priests' instructions seriously.

outline.t: No return to a divorced wife after another marriage
A year at home for the newly married
No millstones as pledges and no kidnapping
Skin diseases and the memory of Miriam
Dignity for borrowers and daily wages for workers
Personal responsibility and justice for the vulnerable
Leaving the gleanings for the poor

doctrines.note: Marriage is guarded from being treated lightly. The divorce law prevents a wife from being passed back and forth, and a new husband is freed from war so that he may bring joy to his wife, a law that values the first year of a marriage.

The chapter shows law as mercy in practice. It protects the poor borrower's dignity, the worker's daily bread, and the gleaner's share of the harvest, and it limits punishment to the guilty person rather than his family.

Israel's ethics rest on its redemption. Because God rescued them from slavery in Egypt, they are to treat the slave, the stranger, and the poor as God treated them. Grace received becomes the motive for justice given.

words.note: Ervah, nakedness or indecency. The phrase in verse 1 is literally a nakedness of a thing, and its meaning was debated already in ancient times. It seems to mean something shameful, but it is probably not adultery, which carried the death penalty in chapter 22.

Keritut, divorce, from a root meaning to cut off. The certificate of divorce was a written document that cut the marriage bond and allowed the woman to remarry. The prophets later use the image when God asks where Israel's certificate of divorce is (Isaiah 50:1).

Avot, a pledge or security for a loan. The chapter uses it four times in verses 10-13, each time limiting what a lender may do. The poor man's pledge is to be returned by nightfall, so that he may sleep in his cloak and bless the lender.

Zakar, to remember. Deuteronomy uses remembering as a moral act. Israel is to remember Miriam's discipline (verse 9) and, above all, its own slavery in Egypt (verses 18 and 22). Memory of God's rescue is what keeps a people generous.

christ: Jesus takes up verse 1 directly. When the Pharisees asked whether a man could divorce his wife for any reason, Jesus answered that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of their hearts, but from the beginning it was not so, and he pointed back to God's design in Genesis 2 (Matthew 19:3-9; Mark 10:2-12). Jesus' parable of the laborers in the vineyard assumes that workers are paid at evening (Matthew 20:8), and James warns that the wages withheld from harvesters cry out to the Lord (James 5:4), echoing verse 15. The gleaning law lies behind the story of Ruth, which leads to David and so to David's greater son. Most deeply, the chapter's motive, remember that you were slaves and the LORD redeemed you, finds its fullest form in the New Testament's call to love because God first loved us and redeemed us in Christ.

hard.q: Does this chapter approve of divorce, and why can't a man remarry his former wife?
hard.a:
Verses 1-4 are a single long case law. The first three verses describe a situation (a man divorces his wife, she remarries, the second marriage ends), and only verse 4 gives the command. So the passage regulates divorce rather than commanding or praising it. Jesus reads it that way, calling it a concession to hardness of heart rather than God's intention.

The reason for forbidding the first husband to take her back is debated. Some interpreters think it protected the woman from being used as a commodity, divorced and reclaimed at a man's whim. Others think it treated a return after a second marriage as a kind of adultery, or as a confusion of family property and relationships. The phrase she has been defiled is difficult; it may describe the first husband's view of her, as though he had declared her unclean when he sent her away. Christians today differ on the grounds for divorce and remarriage (some allow them for adultery and desertion, some more narrowly, some more widely), and this passage is one text among several in that discussion. On every view, the chapter sets limits on divorce rather than making it easy.

questions: Israel was told to remember its own slavery when dealing with the poor. What part of your own story should make you more generous?
A lender could not walk into a borrower's house to pick his pledge. How can you protect the dignity of people who depend on you?
The law set aside the leftovers of the harvest for the poor. What might it look like to leave part of your abundance on purpose for others?
